title: Skill Swap Saturdays
intro: Text 1 is a webpage for a volunteer programme at a community library.

visual.text: You know your phone. They know everything else.
Skill Swap Saturdays — where teenagers and seniors teach each other.
A teenage boy and an elderly woman laugh over a phone. A half-finished rattan basket sits on the table between them.

Your grandmother can fold a ketupat in ten seconds. Can you? Spend one Saturday morning a month with a senior from your neighbourhood. You show them how to make a video call, pay a bill online and spot a scam message. They show you something no app can teach.

visual.title: What one morning looks like
items: 9.30 am — You teach: one phone skill, one-to-one
10.30 am — They teach: cooking, weaving, repairs or dialect
11.30 am — Everyone shares what they learnt

visual.text: “I came to teach Mdm Goh how to pay with her phone. I left knowing how to sew on a button, and with an invitation to lunch every week.” — Irfan, 15
No experience needed. Ages 13 to 18. Counts towards your Values in Action hours.
Sign up by 30 June — places are limited to 40 pairs
Tampines West Community Library · every second Saturday of the month

text2.intro: Text 2 is taken from a blog post by Mdm Goh, a retired tailor who joined the programme.
paragraphs: When my neighbour first told me about these Saturday mornings, I laughed. What could a fifteen-year-old teach a woman who has been sewing since before his parents were born? Quite a lot, it turns out. Irfan showed me how to scan a code at the hawker centre without panicking, and how to send my sister in Penang a voice message instead of waiting for her to call. In return, I taught him to thread a needle and sew on a button so it will not fall off again in a week. Every month I look forward to it more. It is not only the skills. For three hours, someone young listens to me as if what I know still matters.

questions.text: Look at Text 1. Which sentence best states the main message of the webpage?

options.label: A
options.text: Teenagers should help seniors who struggle with their phones.

options.label: B
options.text: Teenagers and seniors each have something worth teaching the other.

options.label: C
options.text: Seniors should pass on traditional crafts before they are forgotten.

scheme.answer: Teenagers and seniors each have something worth teaching the other.

questions.text: Look at the picture in Text 1. How does it support the headline ‘You know your phone. They know everything else.’?

scheme.answer: The boy and the woman share a phone while a half-made rattan basket sits between them, showing that each has a skill to give: he knows the phone, she knows the craft.
accept: The phone stands for what the teenager can teach and the basket for what the senior can teach, so the picture shows the swap the headline describes.
They are laughing together over both a phone and a basket, which shows the two sides learning from each other.

seeds.text: The picture shows the boy with a phone and a half-finished basket on the table, so the boy can teach the phone and the old lady can teach the weaving, just like the headline says.
The phone is the teen's skill and the rattan basket is the senior's skill, so we see both of them have something to teach each other.
It shows that the old woman does not know how to use a phone.
The picture shows two people who look happy together.
A teenage boy and an elderly woman laugh over a phone.
